builder_plan.scenario: Start with one repeated product task that has a measurable failure or cost.
builder_plan.change: Read the methods and identify one change you can isolate in that workflow.
builder_plan.baseline: Your current implementation on the same held-out tasks.
steps: Locate the paper's implementation and check its license, model support, data needs, and hardware requirements. Stop here if you cannot obtain the required artifacts.
Save a small set of representative product tasks and expected outcomes. Keep evaluation tasks out of any training or tuning, and choose quality and cost limits before running.
Run the baseline and the proposed change on identical inputs. Keep other settings fixed and repeat paired runs to expose variation.
Save per-task outputs, failures, timings, and all usage costs. Review regressions before expanding the test.
builder_plan.measure: Successful outcomes, response time, human rework, and total cost per successful task.
builder_plan.decision: Keep the change only if it meets your preselected quality and latency limits and improves the metric you care about after setup and operating costs. Otherwise retain the baseline. This is an exploration plan, not a validated recommendation.

title: e-means: outperforming k-means (in one-tenth the epochs)
summary: e-means replaces Lloyd's k-means iteration (and often k-means++ initialization benefits) with an exponential moving average mini-batch update rule, plus scaling laws that set decay rate and batch size without a hyperparameter sweep, for clustering, quantization, and data curation workloads. The cost is adopting a new implementation and its optimizer-like machinery rather than a mature library routine, with EMA decay interacting with batch size if the prescribed rule is not followed. It can fail if the scaling-law formula does not transfer to embedding distributions or cluster counts outside the evaluated regimes, or if downstream pipelines depend on exact Lloyd-style centroid semantics.
rationale: The method targets a standard clustering workload and claims large speedups with hyperparameter-free configuration, so it merits small-scale validation on the reader's own embeddings before production adoption.

claims.statement: e-means replaces Lloyd's k-means iteration (and often k-means++ initialization benefits) with an exponential moving average mini-batch update rule, plus scaling laws that set decay rate and batch size without a hyperparameter sweep, for clustering, quantization, and data curation workloads. The cost is adopting a new implementation and its optimizer-like machinery rather than a mature library routine, with EMA decay interacting with batch size if the prescribed rule is not followed. It can fail if the scaling-law formula does not transfer to embedding distributions or cluster counts outside the evaluated regimes, or if downstream pipelines depend on exact Lloyd-style centroid semantics.

Matches Lloyd k-means loss at 25 epochs within 1.4 to 2.6 epochs, corresponding to 10-45x GPU wall-clock speedups over state-of-the-art k-means implementations, and frequently converges to lower losses than k-means++.
